<reason>CON won the scope war. From the opening onward, B isolated the case the motion actually bans—somatic, non-heritable edits to a competent adult's own body—and showed that nearly all of PRO's harms (embryos, grandchildren, inheritance, arms races across generations) live on the germline side of a line PRO himself admits is already drawn. PRO's best counter was the unverifiability throughline (A4.4-A4.5: registries can't inspect genomes), but CON broke it twice: first with the "proves too much" reductio (therapeutic somatic gene therapy uses the same invisible edits in the same clinics, and PRO never took that bullet), then with the self-refutation point (if regulators can't detect which line was crossed, they can't detect the edit happened at all, so a ban polices only honest clinics while licensing governs them). PRO's closing never answered the therapy reductio and mostly reasserted the inspection point. Both sides followed the Q/A format properly and grounded claims in ordinary background knowledge rather than fake citations; PRO's clipped opening and clipped CON rebuttal were minor execution costs. CON made the debate easier to decide with a clean burden story and a named victim the proposition criminalizes; PRO never looked her in the eye.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1-B4.4: CON's answer to PRO's unverifiability argument—the dual move that invisibility proves too much (it would ban somatic gene therapy too) and cuts both ways (an undetectable edit makes a ban no more enforceable than a license, only less informed)—decisively cracked PRO's central throughline, and PRO's closing failed to repair it.</best_rebuttal>
